title: Town & Village Joint Meeting
text: Minutes of the Town of Lake George Town Board/Village of Lake George Joint Meeting held on Tuesday, September 29, 2026 at 4:30 p.m. at the Lake George Town Center, 20 Old Post Road, Lake George, New York 12845 Present: Vinnie Crocitto, Supervisor Edward Pagnotta, Jr., Deputy Supervisor Nancy Stannard-Linehan, Councilperson Marisa Muratori, Councilperson Chris Hawley, Councilperson Ray Perry, Mayor Joe Mastrodomenico, Deputy Mayor Jose Filomeno, Trustee Rob Gregor,Trustee Mike Menter, Trustee Also Present: Patty Schuster Town Clerk; Jenn Farrell, Comptroller; Luke Mosseau, Tim Hannigan, Tom McKinney, Gail Corlew, Beth Brundage, Edrie Squires, Thomas Williams, Frank Nestro, Thomas Bellmio, Thomas Bellmio, II, Peter Guidarelli, Nicholas Benjamin, Jessica Benjamin, Doni Smith, Matthew Oswald, Dakota Winch, James Barber, John Cocozza-Hill, Mason Wildermuth, Sandy Cocozza-Spellburg, Francis Cocozza, Todd Earl, Kiernan Murray, Jim McEnaney, Sue McEnaney, Ray Calore, Hank Chrzanowski Supervisor Crocitto opened the meeting at 4:30 p.m. The September 29th Town Village Joint Meeting discussed the formation of a fire district. Tim Hannigan explained that a fire district would simplify liability and taxation, leveling the tax base across Village and Town lines. The district would be governed by a publicly elected Board of Fire Commissioners, responsible for budgeting, training, and maintenance. The proposed budget is estimated at $450,000. Concerns were raised about the impact on fire company operations and morale. The next steps include scheduling a public hearing within 30 days to gather public input and finalize the decision. The meeting discussed the potential formation of a fire district to manage fire protection services more efficiently. Vincent Crocitto highlighted the current budget imbalance, where the Town residents pay 80% of the costs, while the Village residents pay only 20%. The proposed district would allow for better management and financial transparency, with commissioners handling specific roles. The referendum would authorize the district's creation and transfer of the village's LOSAP program. A public hearing is scheduled for October 29 at 5:00 PM. Tom McKinney: To start us off, I'd like to introduce one of my good friends, Tim Hannigan from the Hanningan Law Firm, FASNY Firefighter Association, State of New York. He is also our attorney, so that's how I interact with Tim. Tim and his father Terry are probably the two most versatile people when it comes to fire service legislation, fire service law, and what we can and cannot do. For many years there has been talk about a fire district, what's the difference, so on and so forth. Because I had some conversation with Tim, different things were going on. Rather than guess, rather than listen to me, maybe I might know what I'm talking about, maybe I don't, the fire company decided to spend a little money and talk to Tim and get the answers of what a fire district is, what's the difference, and how does it become, and is that something we're interested? At this point in time, nothing's been done other than a fact-finding mission, and nothing's been said that we are doing this or not doing this. Tonight is what that's all about. So our elected officials will hear what it is, what's the difference, what can happen, what cannot happen, and so on and so forth. And I would ask Tim to address and answer anybody's questions, and probably give you a quick overview of where we are and what happens from here. Tim Hannigan: Thanks for having me. My father and I represent fire districts, fire companies like Lake George that contracts a Village and a Town like it goes now, and we that statewide. I'm also a volunteer firefighter in my hometown in Elsmere, which is just outside of Albany. I've done that for 22 years. So you're here today as the supervisor indicated to talk about this is like the joint meeting, which is kind of the first step in the fire district process. But it's odd that the law requires you to engage in that first step before you can even figure out what the public thinks or really what you as two boards think. So right now you have a village and a village fire department that contracts with a town that has two fire protection districts, and that's key for a couple of reasons. One, if this district was to be formed, I think that the easiest and most readily accessible way to define the fire district would be townwide, encompassing the village and the two fire protection districts into one. It simplifies the liability question for the town and the village, and it also puts firmly and quite easily by defining the geographic bounds of the town, what the fire district is, who the people are that that are that are taxed thereby, and who's protected by the district. A fire district is governed by a publicly elected board of fire commissioners. So the initial board would be appointed by both of your boards. Generally, be five people. That's usually the standard, where in terms of people from the public that you would select. They do not have to be firefighters. They do have to be residents of the new district. So, that's the only qualification. They actually don't even have to be registered voters. They just have to live in the district. But that initial board is appointed by you, and thereafter it takes root and forms on its own. It has elections on the second Tuesday of December every single year, whereupon one commissioner and then any other special items that the district has for election are voted on. But the rule is similar to what the town would do for special elections. They're subject to the same provisions of town law. They are elected public officials. They have to file all those clerks, and they'd have to prepare a budget, which for fire districts that exist now kicks off the third week in October, where they do public budget hearings as in any local government. The greatest benefit I think for the village and the town in forming this is one for your constituents, it will level the tax base across village and town lines. So, right now, I don't know the exact amount, but I'm betting that the town residents pay a little differently, perhaps more than what the village residents do. A fire district across the entire town, or at least as between the village and the town, will levy the playing field as in terms of what is paid per thousand across because you're getting the same fire protection. You're getting the same fire protection now. I just think, all in all likelihood, the rates are different. Two liability concerns. So anything that the fire company does now, the village fire department does now. If they are responding in the in the town, the town owns the liability for that. And if they're responding in the village, the village is liable for that. With the formation of a fire district, which is its own separate political subdivision of the state, any of that liability rests with the fire district. So, in the event that, and we see it thankfully not so much up here where I am, but basically south of Poughkeepsie, is people sue fire departments and fire districts all the time. They sue villages and towns, and usually the town and village don't realize that until they're paid as a defendant, whether it's a motor vehicle accident or somebody claiming to house out correctly, anything like that. So that that whole liability threat is gone. That that all those that's completely off your plate. Same thing for all the volunteer firefighters' benefit loss protection or board workers' comp insurance you provide. That would all be provided by the district, and the board of fire commissioners would sit at the same level as the town board or village board for the purposes of the eyes of the law. But any questions, comments, concerns that either the village received or the town received about fire protection, you would say go very to the five commissioners. The five commissioners are uncompensated. No compensation is allowed per the law, and they are required to go through annual training within 270 days upon appointment or election to office, and then following every election thereafter. Any questions you have. I'm pretty versatile as far as what you want to address and how. Please feel free to ask. Mayor Perry: Can I start? Find five people. Show me those five people that you feel, as a group, are responsible enough. Not that I'm not throwing any shade here. That can understand municipal finance and run a fire department and run a district. Show me those five people, and then we can talk further. Tom McKinney: I actually had given a distribution list in an email of I think 11 or 12 names, some of which were either past members of your fire company, our present members that were chiefs or have some sort of interest in the officer line, as well as I think three that are just general public that have knowledge of budgets and budget hearings and how to do all that. Those people again, I think to reiterate to Tim's point, whatever those five people are, within the first year, have to take the mandatory training about exactly what you're talking about and then every time they're elected. The first year, everybody has to run for office. So the poor guy who has got the one-year class is going to have to take that training three times: once from the appointment, once for his one-year election, and once for his five-year election. Okay, so they have to take it three times in three years, so to your point, they are governed by the state comptroller is the one that pretty much has most of the oversight on how they're trained and what they're training is. So to your point, it's not just a bunch of people who are showing up to think they're doing a good job. These people are trained, have to know, and it is two to three days of training. The training is six hours every time you take it. There was 11 or 12 names. Jim McEnaney was the last one on the list. Councilperson Hawley: To raise point, I mean, it's you talk about people running. You don't get to say until you vote on who's in the town board or village board. So you know, you could end up with just as positive or negative that way too. So you know, I mean, I look around this room. There's five or six people in this room. I wouldn't have any problem with them being on there. And there's certainly a lot more people that aren't here that could certainly step up and do the job. So I don't see that as a problem at all. Mayor Ray Perry: Well, agreed, Chris. But I've had direct experience with four chiefs, and with what four chiefs, and each one, I mean, and Jim's here. He's been fantastic. Everyone that served has been fine, but they need a trained period. And I don't, I just don't understand that the trial by fire is the best way to go about this. I mean, I think we really want to leisurely walk into this. I know there's a time constraints with the October and the November deadlines, but I'm not in a hurry for this. Tim Hannigan: So the board of fire commission is comprised of five plus a treasurer plus a secretary. So the treasurer does not have to reside in the in the district. There's a preference, obviously, much like you have, for it to look within your your geographical boundaries first, and then then go outside. But in recent years, the controller's office is actually standardized through the annual financial report that the town and village have to do. The fire district has to do a similar one, and the coding is actually I mean they've got it down. Kind of go all the way down to any little pencil eraser and coding and how that works. This district would obviously have to file that on an annual basis every year, based on the projected, my anticipation is the budget is over $400,000 total. So the law establishes a threshold at $400,000, requiring an outside external audit annually. So if the budget is over $400,000, they have to retain an independent auditor to audit their books on an ongoing annual basis. If it's under $400,000, then they're not subject to that threshold. They're basically deemed they don't have enough money for New York State purposes, so they don't have to get an audit. For any of our clients that are under 400, we always recommend they do, or at least there's people that are with the Comptroller’s office that will do like a like spot check or at least a review to make sure that you're on track. All of them all have something like that, but 400,000 is a hard threshold in the law. It's generally municipal law 290 Z for fire companies, and it's in the town lot for fire districts. But 400,000 have to have an independent audit perform annually. Tom McKinney: And Ray, to your point about you dealing with four chiefs, you have to remember the chief is in charge of emergencies. He's not in charge of apparatus. He's not in charge of purchasing. He's not in charge of anything to do with maintenance. That all falls back on the district. So now you have a five-year plan all the way through. So that district commissioner isn't just voted in this week trying to get six months behind his belt to figure out what he's doing, and then voted out next year. That all falls back on the district. So the district commissioners are responsible for the operation of the fire company, and the fire department and the fire operations is all the chief. So he's the one that's going to say take that big red truck to that little fire. He is not going to talk about maintenance. He's not going to talk about when to buy tires. He doesn't care about air packs. He doesn't care about training issues as far as who's got what training, what level of training you have to be well level. That's all part of the commissioner's jobs. I don’t know if that helps at all? Mayor Ray Perry: It does. Thank you. Councilperson Muratori: Who owns the assets? Who owns the fire department assets if a fire district forms? Tim Hannigan: If a fire district forms, any assets that are owned by the fire company incorporated as a not-for-profit would be retained by the fire company, or they could be transferred to the district. There's a trigger there where if the assets are all substantially all, that they have to get attorney general approval to do that, but that's for the fire company. With respect to any assets on the village now, or I know there's a bond payment on new aerial. In that case, depending on how you issued the bond, it could be callable, so it's not computable. So in any of those, in any of those cases where you have either like pending bond payments or anything, that's the hardest thing. You also have LOSAP. So, LOSAP would require a mandatory vote of the public on this issue. Because there's a LOSAP program, it would be not only transfer of the LOSAP to the new joint district, but also approval of the overall plan to form the fire district. In other words, if the LOSAP program wasn't involved, then this could be done subject to permissive referendum. There's no mechanism to require a public vote absent that. Councilperson Muratori: So, who owns the property and the firehouse? Tim Hannigan: Yes. Councilperson Muratori: And the fire district would own all the equipment. Tim Hannigan: Yes. Councilperson Muratori: Can they purchase it from the village? Tim Hannigan: No, because the taxpayers of the village already bought that and been paid for it. The fire district is the government as well, so the village rather assign that to the fire district or in the case of like these outstanding bond payments, lease them to the fire district the amount of the bond payments and not to the doctorate issue for the bank. The banks generally when this has occurred in the past, they don't care who the check comes from, so they can even delegate that. Say the check is going to come from the fire district, but it's covering village bond payment number so and so to this amount. So some of those financial matters would have to be worked out. But because the public, the taxpayers, already paid for the building, the apparatus, the gear, and you're substituting the government that's now in charge for that, those are transferred over to the new government entity, providing that it's not a not a gift to any private entity. Councilperson Muratori: So if the biggest bonus is leveling the tax base, so everybody pays the same amount across the board, why go through this whole thing about changing everything about the fire district? Why can't the village and towns make a better deal? Tim Hannigan: So they could make a better deal, but that still doesn't that still doesn't provide liability protection for the town and village. I think that's a bigger that's a bigger benefit than taxpayer openness and transparency as a budget bill. I think it also removes from the village and town's concern, like anything related to fire protection. You're basically putting that you're siloing fire protection in a group that's mission is ensure that fire protection is provided, so that you can focus on any of the newer southern things in the village and town. Mayor Ray Perry: Do you know how many villages do not have fire districts? Or actually, let me let me rephrase that. I'm sorry. How many villages do not own their fire in the state of New York? Tim Hannigan: So the Village of South Corning that we just formed the Corning Joint Fire District. They don't. I'm trying to think what other ones. There'll be a bunch in Long Island that are fire districts. I'm trying. Councilperson Muratori: If there's a large expenditure, is there permissible referendum? Tim Hannigan: Yes. So the fire district's building a bond is actually not as easy as the villages. It's more oversight. So, anytime the village or the fire district wants to either issue a bond or to contract the debt through like an installment purchase contract, depending on the dollar value, they have to go out and actually go through a public referendum process where there'd be either a special election during the year or that could be added as a proposition to their ballot, which is generally how other municipal governments do it at their annual election in December. Anytime they move funds, fire districts generally keep savings funds in capital reserve accounts. Same provisions of law in the five towns. Generally, this is about 6g. In those capital reserve accounts, in the event that a fire district wants to move funds from, let's say, the capital reserve fund for apparatus because they're going to buy a new engine. They have to, subject to permissive referendum, adopt a resolution at a public meeting, pass it, publish notice in the paper for 30 days, allow that time period to expire, and then they can they can move funds. So the same accountability that exists in the general municipal law and the town law for town boards applies to the fire districts. Councilperson Stannard-Linehan: So, so the residents have a lot more say then than they do now. They have no say now. Tim Hannigan: Yes and the residents can go through the permissive referendum process, obviously bring a petition to challenge expenditures. They have maximum say over who controls the provision of fire protection on that board. The fire district commissioners, similar to what the village could do now, because you have a village fire department appoint the chief. Town Law 176A governs the duties of the chief, and that the chief is answerable to the board of fire commissioners. They do clarify that the commissioners have no authority on a fire scene. That's the chief, so commissioners can't intervene or say, you know, put water on that fire day. The chief's in charge at the scene, but the fire district can establish rules, regulations, policies governing the fire district, its operations, its members. All the approval of new members would go through the fire district. A lot of the same functions that occur now would just be taken over by the public elected board. Councilperson

text: VILLAGE/TOWN OF MOUNT KISCO PROPOSED LOCAL LAW #__ OF 2026 A LOCAL LAW TO AMEND CHAPTER 96 – TAXATION OF THE CODE OF THE VILLAGE/TOWN OF MOUNT KISCO Be it enacted by the Village Board of the Village/Town of Mount Kisco of the County of Westchester as follows: Additions are reflected with Underlining, Deletions are reflected within Strikethrough Section 1. Legislative Intent. The Board of Trustees finds that the New York State Legislature has amended § 458-a of the Real Property Tax Law (RPTL) to authorize municipalities to adopt a full exemption from real property taxation for the primary residence of seriously disabled veterans meeting specified eligibility requirements. The Board further finds that the Village has long recognized the sacrifices made by veterans and their families. Consistent with that recognition, the Board desires to provide the fullest exemption authorized by law to those veterans whose service-connected disabilities have resulted in permanent and total disability. The Board also desires to increase the maximum exemption allowable for veterans, combat zone veterans, and disabled veterans under RPTL § 458-a for whom RPTL § 458-a. 11. does not apply The purpose of this Local Law is to amend Chapter 96 of the Code of the Village/Town of Mount Kisco to adopt the optional exemption authorized by RPTL § 458-a. 11., and to adopt a Veterans Alternative Exemption that will increase the maximum exemption allowable authorized by RPTL § 458-a. 2.(d)(ii). Section 2. Authority. This local law is adopted pursuant to Real Property Tax Law § 458-a. Section 3. The Code of the Village/Town of Mount Kisco Chapter 96 Taxation, Article III Real Property Tax Exemptions, is hereby amended to add a new § 96-16.3 Veterans; alternative tax exemption, as follows: § 96-16.3. Veterans; alternative tax exemption. A. Grant of exemption. Pursuant to § 458-a of the Real Property Tax Law (RPTL), qualifying residential real property as defined therein shall be eligible for the veterans alternative exemption as authorized therein. B. Maximum exemption amounts. The Village/Town of Mount Kisco hereby grants the following maximum exemption amounts as authorized by RPTL § 458-a: (1) War Veteran Exemption: $45,000 (2) Combat Veteran Exemption: $30,000. This exemption is in addition to any exemption granted under (1) of this subsection as authorized and permitted under RPTL § 458-a. (3) Disabled Veteran Exemption: $150,000 C. Seriously Disabled Veterans Exemption. Pursuant to RPTL § 458-a. 11., the Village/Town of Mount Kisco hereby grants the full real property tax exemption for seriously disabled veterans authorized therein. Section 4. The Code of the Village/Town of Mount Kisco Chapter 96 Taxation, Article III Real Property Tax Exemptions, is hereby amended to add a new § 96-17.3 Qualifications for veterans; alternative exemption. § 96-17.3. Qualifications for veterans; alternative exemption. Eligibility for the exemptions authorized by § 96-16.3 shall be determined in accordance with Real Property Tax Law (RPTL) § 458-a. No exemption as provided for in § 96-16.3 shall be granted unless all of the applicable qualifications and requirements of RPTL § 458-a shall be met. Section 5. The Code of the Village/Town of Mount Kisco Chapter 96 Taxation, Article III Real Property Tax Exemptions, is hereby amended to add a new § 96-18.3 Application for veterans; alternative exemption. § 96-18.3. Application for veterans; alternative exemption. Applications for the exemptions authorized by § 96-16.3 shall be filed with the Village/Town of Mount Kisco Assessor's Office, which shall determine eligibility and administer such exemptions in accordance with Real Property Tax Law (RPTL) § 458-a. Section 6. The Code of the Village/Town of Mount Kisco Chapter 96 Taxation, Article III Real Property Tax Exemptions, § 96-16. Exemption granted, is hereby amended to be renamed as follows: § 96-16. Senior citizen Eexemption granted. Section 7. Following adoption of this Local Law, the Village Clerk shall notify the New York State Department of Veterans' Services in accordance with Real Property Tax Law (RPTL) § 458-a. 11.(d). Section 8. In the event of any conflict or inconsistency between the provisions of this Local Law and any other provisions of the Code of the Village/Town of Mount Kisco, the provisions of this Local Law shall prevail to the extent necessary to give full force and effect to its provisions. Section 9. If any clause, sentence, paragraph, section or part of this Local Law is declared by a Court of competent jurisdiction to be invalid, such judgment shall not affect, impair or invalidate the remainder thereof, but shall be confined in its operation to said clause, sentence, paragraph, section or part of this Local Law. Section 10. This Local Law shall take effect immediately upon filing in the office of the Secretary of State in accordance with Municipal Home Rule Law Section 27.
